Below is a list of common-area locations where you can place visible, non-audio cameras to enhance safety while respecting guest privacy and staying within most short-term-rental rules. Before installing any device, be sure to:

• Review local and state/provincial surveillance and recording laws (especially regarding audio).  
• Read and comply with your platform’s (Airbnb, VRBO, etc.) full camera-disclosure requirements.  
• Clearly note in your listing all camera locations and post simple “24-hour video surveillance” signage on-site.  
• Never place cameras in private spaces (bedrooms, bathrooms, changing areas).

Recommended camera locations:

1. Front Entrance (exterior)  
   – Captures arrivals/departures without recording inside.  
   – Mount above or beside the door, angled down.  
   – No audio; visible placement deters trespass.

2. Back/Side Door (exterior)  
   – Monitors deliveries, maintenance staff, service access.  
   – High-corner placement overlooking the threshold.

3. Main Hallway or Corridor  
   – Position a camera up high at one end, covering the full corridor.  
   – Ensures visibility of who goes to/from private rooms without filming inside.

4. Stairwell (top or bottom)  
   – Covers vertical movement between floors.  
   – Mount on a wall or ceiling opposite the first few steps.

5. Shared Outdoor Areas (patio, deck, pool, driveway)  
   – One or two wide-angle cameras to cover gathering spots or parking.  
   – Keep them outside property lines or clearly on your premises.

6. Common-Use Laundry/Utility Room (if provided)  
   – Only if this room is exclusively shared and not used for personal tasks.  
   – Visible placement by the door, no audio recording, and disclosed to guests.

7. Entry Vestibule or Mudroom  
   – If you have a small foyer before main living space, a camera here sees guest entry without recording the living room.

Additional best practices:

• Avoid hidden or inconspicuous cameras; use dome or bullet housings so guests see them.  
• Do not install microphones—audio recording often requires two-party consent.  
• Secure all footage with encrypted storage; restrict access to authorized staff only.  
• Keep signs brief (“Video surveillance in operation”) and place them at main entrances.  
• Update your property’s rules and listing to state exactly where cameras are and what they monitor.

By confining cameras to entryways, corridors and outdoor/common spots—and by fully disclosing their presence—you’ll strike the right balance between guest safety and privacy. Always double-check local statutes or consult a hospitality attorney if you’re unsure about specific recording regulations in your jurisdiction.
